name: Ahmad Shawqi
bio: Ahmad Shawqi was born in Cairo in 1285 AH (1868 CE) and grew up in the shadow of Egypt's ruling house; he wrote that he had heard his father trace the family back “to the Kurds, then the Arabs”. He studied law in Egypt and then in Montpellier, where Khedive Tawfiq sent him, and came back to head the European bureau at the court of Khedive Abbas Hilmi; when Abbas was deposed during the First World War, Shawqi was told to live somewhere other than Egypt, spent 1915 to late 1919 in Spain, where he wrote of the Arabs' glory in al-Andalus and of his longing for Egypt, and on his return sat in the Senate. He wrote praise, love poems, elegies and descriptions, and then poems on the events of Egypt, the East and the Muslim world that everyone repeated, collected as al-Shawqiyyat; he was also the first to excel at verse drama in Arabic, with plays such as The Death of Cleopatra and Majnun Layla. Long called the Prince of Poets, he was crowned with the title in 1927, when he reissued al-Shawqiyyat and a celebration in his honour drew delegations from across the Arab world; Hafiz Ibrahim declared: “Prince of rhymes, I have come to pledge allegiance.” He died in Cairo in 1351 AH (1932 CE).
